title: James
subtitle: faith that works, from the brother of the Lord
lead: James is a short letter of five chapters, written in vivid Greek to "the twelve tribes in the Dispersion". It reads less like Paul's letters than like Proverbs or the Sermon on the Mount: a string of sharp sayings and pictures about trials, wisdom, the rich and the poor, the tongue, prayer and patience. Its writer calls himself only "James, a slave of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ", and the church has long identified him as James the brother of Jesus, leader of the church in Jerusalem.

The letter is best known for one sentence: "So you see that it is by works that a person is justified, and not by faith alone" (2:24). That line made Luther call James "an epistle of straw" beside the books that preach Christ most clearly, and it has stood at the center of the debate between the churches ever since. Read on its own terms, James is a passionate call to a faith that shows itself in deeds: feeding the hungry, honoring the poor, taming the tongue, praying for the sick and bringing back the wanderer.
facts: "James" (1:1), traditionally James the brother of Jesus, leader of the Jerusalem church. Many critical scholars: a later writer using his name.
Traditional view: before James' death about AD 62, perhaps in the 40s or 50s. Many critical scholars: late first or early second century.
Written to scattered communities, most likely Jewish believers in Jesus outside the land of Israel, many of them poor
A letter in form (greeting only), in substance a wisdom sermon of short sayings and exhortations
Greek, polished and rich in images

audience.to: "The twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (1:1). The phrase was the Jewish name for the scattered people of Israel living outside the land, and the letter's world is thoroughly Jewish: its readers meet in a "synagogue" (2:2), know the law and the Shema, and take Abraham, Rahab, Job and Elijah as their own. They are mostly poor: day laborers whose wages are held back (5:4), people dragged into court by the rich (2:6), brothers and sisters without enough food or clothing (2:15). Some are traders planning a year's business in another city (4:13). Their meetings are troubled by favoritism toward the wealthy (2:1-4), quarrels and envy (4:1-2), slander (4:11), and teachers competing for honor (3:1, 14).
audience.why: To call a pressured community to a faith that is whole and undivided. James answers the temptations of the poor (to blame God for their trials, to envy and flatter the rich, to grumble against each other, to seek revenge) and the temptations of the comfortable (to claim faith without helping the needy, to plan without God). His answer is wisdom from God, endurance, mercy and prayer, in the hope of the Lord's coming. Knowing the readers explains the letter's sharpest lines: the attack on favoritism was written to the poor who were honoring their oppressors, and "faith without works is dead" was written to people who wished the hungry well and sent them away.
views: The twelve tribes are Jewish Christians of the Dispersion, written to by James from Jerusalem, much as Jerusalem sent the letter of Acts 15:23 to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. The "synagogue" of 2:2 and the Jewish texture of the whole letter favor this view.

The twelve tribes are all Christians, Jewish and Gentile, seen as the renewed people of God living as exiles in the world, as 1 Peter 1:1 seems to use "Dispersion". On this view the letter is a circular letter to the church at large.

If the letter was written after James' death, its readers were churches that honored James' memory, perhaps in Syria or Palestine, and the faith-and-works passage may answer people who had taken Paul's teaching as permission to neglect good works.

authorship: James the brother of Jesus wrote the letter. He was known by his name alone and had authority over Jewish believers everywhere. Galatians 1:19 calls him "the brother of the Lord"; Acts shows him leading the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13; 21:18); Josephus (Antiquities book 20, quoted by Eusebius) and Hegesippus (also quoted by Eusebius) tell of his death in Jerusalem. The letter's Jewish world, its closeness to Jesus' sayings, and its picture of poor laborers and early and late rains fit him. Some who hold this view think James used a helper to write the Greek. Some, such as Calvin, thought the writer was the apostle James son of Alphaeus, often identified with the Lord's brother.

A widely held view in scholarship is that the letter is pseudonymous: a later writer used James' name. The arguments: the polished Greek, with no evidence that James had a Greek education; possible dependence on 1 Peter; an apparent answer to a later misuse of Paul; and the letter's slow acceptance in the early church. Eusebius (about AD 325) wrote that it "is disputed" and that "not many of the ancients have mentioned it", and Jerome reported that some claimed it was "published by some one else under his name". Those who hold this view date it from the late first to the mid-second century.

Others propose that many of the sayings go back to James himself, and that his followers collected and edited them into the present letter after his death. This would explain both the early, Jewish character of the teaching and the polished Greek.
outline: Greeting to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion
Trials and wisdom; the low and the rich; tested, not tempted; every good gift
Hearing and doing the word; true religion
No favorites in the assembly; the royal law; mercy over judgment
Faith without works is dead: Abraham and Rahab
Wisdom from below and from above
Wars within; friendship with the world; humble yourselves; do not judge
Patience until the Lord comes; no oaths
Prayer, the anointing of the sick, confession, Elijah, and bringing back the wanderer

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads James as a letter to real communities of poor believers under pressure from wealthy landowners and merchants, in the world of first-century Judaism and the Roman east, and asks what the letter meant to them.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks who wrote the letter and when (James of Jerusalem, a later writer, or an edited collection of his teaching), how it relates to Paul, and why it was slow to be accepted. Holds the question of authorship open and weighs the arguments.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads James as wisdom teaching and exhortation (paraenesis): short units linked by catchwords, vivid images, an imagined opponent in the style of the diatribe, and themes that open in chapter 1 and return at the end.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads James as a Jewish wisdom writing alongside Proverbs, Sirach and the Wisdom of Solomon: the Shema, the whole Torah, Abraham's test, the evil inclination, Elijah's prayer, and the law of wages.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Follows how the churches have read James: its slow acceptance into the canon, Luther's "epistle of straw", the Council of Trent's use of 2:24 and 5:14-15, the Orthodox Holy Unction, and the long debate over faith and works.

sections.b:
James is meant to be heard, not studied in pieces. Read it aloud in one sitting (the Plain runs to about 2,500 words) and listen for the words that come back: trial, endurance, complete, wisdom, double-minded, rich and poor, the word, doers, the tongue, judge, mercy, prayer. Chapter 1 sounds most of them in short order; chapters 2 to 5 develop them one by one.

James teaches like a Jewish sage. He does not build long arguments as Paul does. He piles up sayings and pictures: a wave of the sea, a wildflower, a mirror, a bit and a rudder, a forest fire, a spring, a fig tree, a puff of steam, rust, a farmer waiting for rain. He often argues with an imagined listener ("But someone will say", 2:18), and he is not afraid to scold ("You empty man", 2:20; "You adulteresses!", 4:4).

sections.h: James and the teaching of Jesus
sections.b:
James names Jesus only twice (1:1; 2:1), yet no letter in the New Testament sounds more like Jesus' own teaching, especially the Sermon on the Mount:

Joy in trials (1:2; Matthew 5:11-12). Ask and it will be given (1:5; Matthew 7:7). Doers, not only hearers (1:22; Matthew 7:24-26). The poor heirs of the kingdom (2:5; Luke 6:20). Mercy to the merciful (2:13; Matthew 5:7). A tree known by its fruit (3:12; Matthew 7:16). Peacemakers (3:18; Matthew 5:9). Friendship with the world (4:4; Matthew 6:24). Laughter turned to grief (4:9; Luke 6:25). Do not judge (4:11; Matthew 7:1). Moth and rust (5:2-3; Matthew 6:19). The Judge at the doors (5:9; Matthew 24:33). No oaths, let your yes be yes (5:12; Matthew 5:34-37).

James almost never quotes Jesus word for word. He has absorbed the teaching and speaks it in his own voice, which some take as a sign that the writer knew it from the oral tradition before the Gospels were written.

The famous tension is in 2:14-26: James says "it is by works that a person is justified, and not by faith alone" (2:24), while Paul says "a person is justified by faith, apart from works of the law" (Romans 3:28), and both use Abraham. The chapter page for chapter 2 sets the two side by side, explains how the key words differ, and gives each church's reading in its own words. The short version: almost every church today holds that James and Paul do not finally contradict each other, but they explain the agreement differently, and that difference is one of the deepest lines between the Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions.

James was slow to be accepted everywhere. Eusebius of Caesarea, writing about AD 325, called it the first of the "catholic" (general) letters but added that it "is disputed; at least, not many of the ancients have mentioned it", though "read publicly in very many churches" (Church History 2.23.25); in his list of books he placed it among the disputed writings "which are nevertheless recognized by many" (3.25.3). Jerome noted that some thought it was written by someone else in James' name. By the end of the 300s it was accepted in the Greek and Latin churches.

Luther, in his German New Testament of 1522, gave James a preface praising it as "a good book, because it sets up no doctrines of men but vigorously promulgates the law of God", but denying it was by an apostle and placing it with Hebrews, Jude and Revelation at the end, apart from "the true chief books". In his general preface of the same year he called it "an epistle of straw" compared with John, Paul's letters and 1 Peter, a sentence later dropped from his Bible. The Council of Trent (1546) listed "one of the apostle James" among the sacred and canonical books, and the Westminster Confession (1646) lists "The Epistle of James" among the books "given by inspiration of God". Every church today has James in its New Testament.

James is thoroughly Jewish. It addresses Israel's twelve tribes, calls the meeting a synagogue, assumes the whole Torah is binding (2:10), quotes the love command (Leviticus 19:18) and the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), and draws its examples from Abraham, Rahab, Job, Elijah and the prophets. Its closest relatives are Jewish wisdom books: Proverbs, Sirach and the Wisdom of Solomon. Leviticus 19, the chapter of the love command, runs through the letter. Luke Timothy Johnson ("The Use of Leviticus 19 in the Letter of James", 1982, reprinted in Brother of Jesus, Friend of God, 2004) traced it verse by verse: no false oaths (Leviticus 19:12; James 5:12), wages paid the same day (19:13; 5:4), no favoritism (19:15; 2:1, 9), no slander (19:16; 4:11), and reproving a neighbor (19:17; 5:20), beside the love command itself (19:18; 2:8). He concluded, as Mark E. Taylor quotes him, that James made "conscious and sustained use" of Leviticus 19:12-18.

prompts: A hand-drawn scroll sketch: a bearded man in a first-century tunic glances into a small round bronze mirror, then turns away, his reflection fading; beside him another figure bends close over an open scroll of the law, lit warmly. Ancient manuscript texture, ochre and charcoal lines like a cave drawing, soft frayed edges, no hard border.

A tiny flame drawn in red ochre at the tip of a stylized tongue, spreading across a hillside forest sketched in fine brown ink; above, a horse with a bit and a ship with a small rudder in the margins like hieroglyphs. Modern line art mixed with ancient manuscript style on a curling scroll, soft edges.

Day laborers with sickles in a golden wheat field at dusk, their cries drawn as rising lines toward the sky; in the corner a rich man's chest of coins crusted with rust and a moth-eaten robe. Sketched on parchment, earth tones, cave-painting figures, soft torn edges.

Elders of an early church gathered at a sickbed in a lamp-lit stone room, one pouring olive oil from a small clay flask onto the forehead of a sick man while the others pray with raised hands. Hand-drawn on a scroll, warm sepia, soft edges, no frame.

traditions.q: Is the Letter of James fully part of the Bible, with the same authority as the other books?
views: Yes. The Council of Trent's decree on the canonical Scriptures (session 4, 1546) lists "one of the apostle James" among the books to be received "as sacred and canonical".

Lutherans have it in their Bibles, but Luther himself did not count it among "the true chief books": "I will not have him in my Bible to be numbered among the true chief books, though I would not thereby prevent anyone from including or extolling him as he pleases" (Preface to James and Jude, 1522). He kept it in his Bible all the same. His general preface of 1522 also called it "an epistle of straw" beside John, Paul and 1 Peter; that sentence was removed from the preface in every edition of his German Bible after 1537 (Martin Foord, Themelios 45.2).
Yes. The Westminster Confession lists "The Epistle of James" among the books "given by inspiration of God to be the rule of faith and life" (1.2).

reading: Dan G. McCartney, James (Baker Exegetical Commentary on the New Testament, 2009)
A careful evangelical commentary on the Greek text, with a full discussion of authorship.
Dale C. Allison Jr., A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Epistle of James (T&T Clark, 2013)
A full critical commentary on the Greek text in the International Critical Commentary series.
Scot McKnight, The Letter of James (New International Commentary on the New Testament, 2011)
A commentary that places Torah observance at the heart of James' ethics.
Peter H. Davids, The Epistle of James (New International Greek Testament Commentary, 1982)
A classic commentary on the Greek text.
Luke Timothy Johnson, The Letter of James (Doubleday, 1996)
A literary and historical commentary, with a long history of how the letter has been read.
Richard Bauckham, James: Wisdom of James, Disciple of Jesus the Sage (Routledge, 1999)
James as a Jewish wisdom teacher in the tradition of Jesus.
